text: Morning news: at the New Year party, every department has to perform a number. Your team voted unanimously that the newest hire will do it. That’s you.
The party chat is voting on a theme. “The ’90s” is winning, “Pajama Party” is right behind. Yours is the deciding vote, and you don’t own decent pajamas.
The party is in full swing. The host with the mic is looking for a volunteer for “Who Can Put On Five Sweaters Fastest.” His eyes land on you.
At the party, Lidia from Accounting has spent the whole evening telling you about her summer-house renovation. Forty minutes in, she’s only reached the foundation.
right: Hear it out to the roof

text: The morning after the party. Photos are already in the group chat, and in one of them you’re hugging a ficus and singing into it like a mic. It’s racking up reactions.
HR wants everyone to fill in a two-page form: “My Expectations for the Office Party.” Question five: “Describe the ideal party game in verse.”
Marina whispers that there’ll be a raffle at the party, but only for people who hand in their report by Friday. Your report is half done.
The party ended at midnight. Coworkers from a nearby area suggest splitting one taxi four ways. You’d be dropped off last.
It’s Gosha from Logistics’ birthday. You barely know him, but the card has made its way around to you. There’s room for exactly one word.
The birthday girl brought cake for the whole team. The last slice has been sitting on the plate for an hour. Everyone eyes it, nobody dares.
The team decided to serenade the birthday boy with a guitar. Everyone’s singing, nobody knows the words. Someone hands you the lyrics and nudges you to center stage.
The office manager asks you to keep the team’s birthday calendar. Simple job: don’t forget anyone. Price of a mistake: eternal resentment.
It’s your birthday. Office tradition says the birthday person feeds everyone. Your budget covers either pizza for all or a decent lunch for a week.
Coworkers want to keep celebrating your birthday at a cafe tonight. The birthday person pays, naturally. Stand-up is at nine tomorrow.
The boss forgot a colleague’s birthday and, last minute, tells you to “organize something.” The celebration is in twenty minutes.
You arrive to find your desk buried in balloons. Lovely, but you can’t reach your laptop, and a client call starts in ten minutes.
After the party, everyone heads to karaoke. You draw a duet with the boss: a song about heartbreak. He’s already holding the second mic.
right: Pass the mic to a coworker

text: The party theme is “Hollywood.” Coworkers ordered costumes; all you have is your fancy reindeer sweater. Two days to go.
You’ve been named party photographer. The camera isn’t yours, the manual is in Japanese, and the boss wants it “magazine-cover quality.”
The organizer shows you the seating chart. You’re between the CEO and his mother-in-law, who came along “for company.”
Toasts are going around the table. Three people until your turn. Everyone’s talking about “team spirit,” and fresh ideas ran out two toasts ago.
right: Give a speech on the mission

text: Coworkers ask what you’d like for your birthday. You want headphones, but that’s a lot for everyone to chip in. Be honest?
Oleg the sysadmin asked for no birthday fuss. The team’s planning a surprise anyway, and they want you to distract him in the server room.
At the Friday buffet for the company anniversary, the snacks vanished in five minutes. The CEO hasn’t even arrived. Buy pizza with your own money?
The team is rehearsing a flash mob for the party. Every morning at eight, before work. The choreographer is a very strict sales manager.
right: Claim you have two left feet

text: There’s a contest for the best greeting for the company anniversary. Prize: an extra day off. You’d have to write it on company time.
At the party you win the raffle’s grand prize: a giant teddy bear as tall as a person. You’re taking the subway home.
The facilities manager asks you to help hang garlands for the party. The stepladder wobbles and the garland is tangled like earbuds in a pocket.
The team is planning a birthday surprise for the boss. Someone has to come in at 7 a.m. to decorate her office. Everyone looks at the youngest.
This year’s party is online: video-chat games until 10 p.m. Cameras must stay on — turning yours off is “disrespecting the team.”
Sveta hints that “last year everyone forgot her.” Her birthday is next week, and somehow you’re now in charge of it.
Monday after the party. Half the team is “working from home.” The boss asks you to run stand-up for him.
The office manager needs you to pick napkin colors for the party: “turquoise” or “mint.” This decision has been pending all morning.
right: Run a poll in the chat

text: The party. A slow song starts, and a coworker from the next department stands before you, hand outstretched. Everyone’s watching.
You’re invited to the CFO’s milestone birthday. You’ve seen him twice, both times in the elevator. Attendance is “highly encouraged.”
The team is recording a farewell video for a colleague who moved away. They want you to say something touching. Camera’s rolling, take five.
Evening. Half a birthday cake sits in the fridge. The cleaner empties the fridge at eight tomorrow. Take it home?
The union gave the team $50 for a celebration. You’re supposed to spend it so “everyone’s happy.” There are fifteen people.
The boss announces the party is moving to Saturday “so we don’t get distracted from work.” You bought tickets for Saturday ages ago.
Party at a restaurant. On the way out, your jacket is gone, and there’s a similar one left on the rack. You lost your ticket long ago.
left: Wait for it to get sorted

text: The boss wants a party report for the CEO: “What worked, what to improve.” Be honest about the sweater game?
Coworkers are celebrating a birthday right in the middle of your urgent task. It smells like pizza, everyone’s calling you over. Deadline in two hours.
The party’s winding down. The CEO just arrived and wants to “hang out with the young folks.” The young folks are you and the intern.
You get a birthday card from the company. It’s signed to “Dear Employee.” They didn’t even fill in your name. Coworkers giggle.
HR invites you to join the “Celebrations Committee.” They promise it’s “fun and prestigious.” It meets during lunch break.
Team building starts at 9:00 in the woods. The coach hands out blindfolds: “You’ll fall backward and your colleagues will catch you.” The catchers are from Accounting.
Team escape room: get out in an hour. You found the key in five minutes, but the captain asks you to “slow down and let everyone take part.”
left: Give the key to the captain

text: Team retreat. Around the fire, everyone shares “their biggest fear.” It’s your turn, and the guitar has gone quiet.
The team-building bus leaves at 7:30. The only window seat left is next to a coworker who spends every trip polling people on their five-year goals.
Rope course, twenty feet up. The boss already finished and is waving from below. Your turn, and your legs won’t cooperate.
Team game: come up with a team name. Options: “Sales Dragons” and “Reporting Tigers.” You’ve got a funnier one, but it’s riskier.
Evening at the retreat. Groups take turns in the sauna, and both groups invite you along for “a serious talk about the project.”
Day two of the retreat. The boss is personally leading 7 a.m. exercises in a dewy meadow. Half the team is hiding in their cabins.
Tug-of-war: your department vs. IT. The sysadmins pull silently and mightily. The boss yells “Not one step back!” Your palms are on fire.
The psychologist asks everyone to draw “the team as an animal.” Coworkers draw lions and eagles. You honestly drew a sloth.
The retreat disco runs till 2 a.m. Rafting is scheduled for 8:00. Coworkers drag you to dance “just one song.”
HR sends a survey: “Rate the team building from 1 to 10.” It’s anonymous, yet the link somehow contains your name.
Cooking team building: the department makes pasta under a chef’s eye. You’re on sauce. The sauce is burnt, and the chef is coming to taste it.
Role-play: “Negotiating with Aliens.” You got the alien, so you have to speak a made-up language in front of the whole department.
The bus heads back from the retreat. Coworkers start a sing-along, and it’s going to be a long one. Three hours to the city; your headphones are dead.
Kayaking trip. You’re paired with the boss. He sits in the back, gives orders, and doesn’t paddle. The kayak is slowly drifting into the bushes.
Game: “Pay a coworker a compliment.” You drew the one you’ve argued with all week. He’s waiting, arms crossed.
Company sports day. Your team is one player short for soccer. You last saw a ball in school, but they only need you to “just stand in goal.”
Night orienteering with flashlights. Your team is lost, the accountant has the compass, and he’s sure north is wherever the Wi-Fi is.
Announcement: team building on Saturday, “attendance voluntary but noted.” On Saturday you have a hike with friends planned a month ago.
Task: build a bridge from pasta and tape that holds a mug. The team has argued over the blueprint for half an hour, and you have an idea.
Team-building results are in. Your team came last and gets the “Will to Win” prize: a box of rubber ducks.
The facilitator gets everyone in a circle holding hands to shout a motto. You have to come up with the motto while everyone waits.
The retreat game is “Secret Friend”: secretly do something nice for someone. You drew the boss. What’s a nice secret thing for a boss?
Barbecue at the retreat. You’re on the grill because “young people have sharper eyes.” Half the meat is already charcoal, and people are hungry.
Group photo time. The photographer lines everyone up and puts you in the center. Problem: you just fell in a puddle during the relay race.
You’re tasked with buying everything for team building from a 40-item list. You’ll be reimbursed “after approval.” The total is half your salary.
Tent night. You’re bunking with a coworker who reportedly snores like a tractor. The only other free spot is in the boss’s car.
Company trivia night. Your team is second, with one soccer question left. Only you know the answer, but the captain is already writing his.
Day two of the retreat. The boss announces a three-hour “efficiency masterclass,” while outside there’s sunshine and a lake.
Egg-and-spoon race. Your team is winning, but you just passed the boss, and he’s visibly upset. Twenty yards to the finish.
The coach asks everyone to rate coworkers’ contributions in writing. The boss will see the lists. Petya spent the whole day on his phone.
The team-building coach calls at 8 a.m. and wants “your personal motto” by lunch. No motto, no retreat, apparently.
Interdepartmental laser tag. You’re in an ambush spot, and walking right past is the head of the next department — the one who decides your bonus.
At the campfire, a sales guy is on his twelfth self-written song. Everyone is sneaking yawns. He asks: “One more?”
Painting team building: each department creates one oil painting together. You got the sky. The sky came out green, and coworkers are already adding clouds.
The coach asks for “one trait that holds you back at work.” The boss is carefully writing the answers in a notebook.
The retreat ended Sunday at 10 p.m. The boss reminds everyone Monday stand-up is at eight “as usual.”
right: Come in half an hour late

text: An African drumming workshop for “team cohesion.” You got the biggest drum. Five minutes in, your head is pounding.
right: Tap it gently with a finger

text: Chat poll: team building at a spa or an obstacle course? The boss voted obstacle course. It’s a tie so far.
After team building, three coworkers need a ride, and you have a car. They live in three different corners of the city, and you live in a fourth.
Lunch at the retreat: the boss orders “for everyone.” He picked aspic and cold beet soup. You eat neither.
Yoga team building: the instructor asks you to “release all work thoughts.” Right then your phone buzzes: a client message.
After the retreat, HR wants everyone to record a video review “with emotion” for the company website. Film at home, due by morning.
The team is racing through a giant crossword. You know the capital of Burkina Faso, but a coworker already wrote in a different word.
Nina from Accounting is going around with an envelope: “$10 each for the facilities manager’s gift.” You don’t know who that is, but the envelope is in front of you.
New collection in the Gifts chat: a wedding gift for a manager from another office. It’s the third collection this month, and payday is two weeks away.
You’re collecting money for the boss’s gift. It’s evening, the envelope is $40 short, and nobody wrote down who didn’t pay.
right: Do a roll call in the chat

text: The team can’t pick a farewell gift for a departing colleague: a blanket or a spa voucher. The debate started at 9 a.m. You get the final say.
The team chipped in for a coffee machine for the boss. That evening you learn she ordered the exact same model for herself yesterday.
A card for the CEO is going around. Above you: “Sincerely yours,” “Best regards,” and “Hugs.” What should a newbie write?
The team’s gift is late: the courier is stuck in traffic, and the presentation is at nine tomorrow. He offers to bring it to your place at 11 p.m.
Someone put a button in the gift envelope instead of money. Everyone’s a suspect. The envelope was kept on your desk.
After work you’re told to buy “something classy” for $100. The store closes in forty minutes, and you have zero ideas.
The office has been collecting “for a kettle” for a year. The money was raised long ago, there’s no kettle, and the collector just smiles at every question.
The gift is bought; wrapping is your job. Floral paper, the tape is running out, and the box is round. The presentation is in the morning.
right: Fuss over a bow till midnight

text: The intern is leaving after three months. Nobody suggests getting him anything. You’re the only one he ever helped with spreadsheets.
The boss asks you to pick a holiday gift for a key client. The budget is modest, and the client collects expensive tea.
Evening. Nobody signed the card for tomorrow’s milestone birthday, and it’s on your desk. Sign for everyone in different handwriting?
Coworkers are debating whether to chip in $10 or $20 for a gift. You earn the least, but you’d rather not admit it.
At his birthday, a coworker got identical barbecue sets from two departments. He looks at you — you bought one of them.
You were asked to track who paid for gifts. A month later, it’s a list of chronic debtors, including the boss.
Office Secret Santa. You drew the chief accountant, who terrifies you. The limit is $10, and gifts are due tomorrow morning.
Your Secret Santa gave you a book: “How to Stop Being Late.” The whole office watched you open it.
Friday night, new chat message: “Urgent! Chip in for flowers, Galina Petrovna is in the hospital.” Nobody knows who Galina Petrovna is.
The boss opened the team’s gift — an embroidery kit — and said a polite “Mmm.” You picked the gift.
The gift collection is cash only: “transfers are hard to count.” You haven’t carried cash in three years, and the nearest ATM is two blocks away.
You’re writing the card text for the boss’s gift from everyone. Coworkers in the chat have already pitched eight contradictory wishes.
A coworker with a birthday brought in his own gift wish list, with prices and links. Everything costs triple the usual.
right: Chip in for the big one

text: The night before the presentation, it turns out the team’s gift is with a coworker who just left on a week’s vacation. Stores are still open.
right: Give a card and a promise

text: Auntie Valya the cleaner has worked here twenty years, and it’s her milestone birthday. Nobody announced a collection; you found out by chance.
Coworkers always bring souvenirs from vacation for everyone. Your vacation is over, and you forgot to buy anything.
The boss hands out holiday gifts. You got an ice-fishing kit with an auger. He clearly mixed up the boxes.
A coworker still hasn’t paid you back for covering his share of a gift a month ago. It’s a small sum, but it stings.
The team is giving the departing boss a “memory album.” Everyone needs to send a photo. You’ve worked here three weeks.
You’re supposed to buy flowers for a morning celebration. The florist near home is closed, and the subway stall only sells carnations.
A new coworker loudly declares she never chips in for gifts on principle. Everyone turns to you — you’re new here too.
A coworker just became a mom. The team is collecting, and you’re picking the gift. The baby store has eight kinds of stroller rattles.
The boss announces: “Chipping in for the CEO’s gift, $40 each.” He forgot to chip in himself, and you’ll have to remind him.
The gift you picked for a coworker was a smash hit. Now the team wants you to pick every gift for everyone, forever.
Two coworkers ask to be “added” to your gift for a mutual acquaintance. They’ll pay you later. Their “later” usually never comes.
The coworker’s gift was ordered online. At 9 p.m.: “Order canceled, out of stock.” The celebration is tomorrow at ten.
For the holiday, the boss gave the team a huge painting of himself. It has to go somewhere. The only free wall is above your desk.
A coworker jokingly asks what to get you for your housewarming. You dream of a vacuum cleaner, but that’s a bit awkward.
Someone put a note in the birthday envelope: “Owe you, will pay.” The handwriting looks a lot like the boss’s.
The team gave you a gift card to a store that closed last week. They’re waiting for delight; you just found out.
The boss’s gift collection has dragged on for a week. That evening you learn the occasion was yesterday. The team waits for someone to tell the boss.
The team chipped in for a giant chocolate cake for the boss. The boss is on a diet. The cake was delivered to your place, and you have to bring it in.
You got perfume for your birthday that you can’t stand. The giver asks every day whether you like it.
A giant poster-card for the director. You’re assigned to draw it because “your profile pic is pretty.”
Whispers in the smoking area: Andrey the manager and Katya the designer have gone to lunch together three days running and come back with matching coffees.
Ira tells you, in strictest confidence, that someone in Sales has a secret crush on you. No name: “Three guesses.”
In the elevator one evening, you walk in on two coworkers who were clearly holding hands and jumped apart. Next morning they act like strangers.
For Valentine’s Day, the office set up a box for anonymous valentines. You got four, all in the accountant’s handwriting.
After the party, a rumor spreads that you went home with someone from IT. Really, they just gave you a ride to the subway.
Everyone’s sure the boss is having an affair with his assistant. They send you to “casually pop into” his office to check. It’s awkward to refuse.
A courier delivers a huge bouquet addressed to you. No note. The whole office freezes and stares, awaiting an explanation.
A coworker accidentally posts in the group chat a message clearly not meant for everyone: “Miss you, kitten.” Deleted a second later. You saw it.
Someone leaves a chocolate bar on your desk every morning. It’s been two weeks. Coworkers are placing bets on who it is.
A coworker from the next department offers to walk you to the subway “since it’s on the way.” It’s honestly not on his way at all.
Zoya the gossip asks if it’s true you had lunch with the new marketer. You did. With the sysadmin as well.
Tanya is jealous of her husband, who works in the next department, and the new intern. She asks you to “keep an eye” on them.
At a cafe one evening, you spot the boss clearly on a date. He sees you too. You both freeze, menus in hand.
Two coworkers whose romance the whole office whispered about announce their wedding. You’re the only one who never noticed.
You find an unsigned love letter in the printer. It’s been there an hour, and the department’s print queue is about to kick in.
A coworker you’ve had a crush on for a month invites you to the movies after work. At 8 a.m. you have a big presentation for the boss.
At lunch, coworkers are discussing two colleagues’ office romance so loudly — and the two of them are at the very next table.
The new manager keeps coming to your desk “to ask about the spreadsheet.” It’s a simple spreadsheet. Coworkers exchange looks and smile.
Evening, rain. A coworker who reportedly likes you offers you a ride. Half the department is smoking by the entrance.
Word reaches you that you’re dating the courier, since he always delivers your packages first. The packages are toner cartridges.
Coworkers want you to sign a card “from the whole team” for the woman the boss is rumored to be seeing. They want the boss to sign first.
You’ve been added to a secret “Team Gossip” chat. The very first message speculates about your direct manager’s love life.
Two coworkers who recently broke up are arguing over every point in the meeting. It’s been two hours. They want you to “moderate.”
An anonymous admirer declares their feelings for you on the company intranet. Everyone can see the post, including the CEO.
right: Ask a moderator to delete it

text: At the team party, a coworker who had too much “special lemonade” loudly confesses he’s “had feelings” for someone on the team. Everyone looks at you.
A coworker tells you she’s dating the head of the next department and asks you to keep quiet. An hour later, everyone knows — except you.
Your officemates started dating and now whisper for hours. Work is impossible, and your desk sits exactly between them.
A coworker wants to set you up on a blind date with her cousin. Saying no means offending her for the rest of your career.
Two coworkers in love are running your joint project. They had a fight, and now each one asks you to pass messages to the other.
The office manager knows everyone’s private life. Today she offers to tell you why the person who had your job before you left.
Friday night at a bar, you spot a married coworker with a stranger. He waves and introduces her: “My sister.”
There’s a rumor you got a bonus because the boss “likes” you. You got it for a report that took you a week.
At the cooler you catch the end of a sentence: “...and then she tells him: not at work!” Coworkers fall silent and look at you.
A coworker wants to set up two single colleagues and asks you to help: invite both to a “casual” dinner for three, then slip away.
A stranger calls your work phone demanding to know who his wife, your coworker, is having lunch with. She’s standing right next to you.
The boss has started praising you in front of everyone suspiciously often. Coworkers whisper. You just do good work.
left: Ask him to tone it down

text: In a company photo, you ended up next to a coworker, and it looks like you’re holding hands. The photo is already on the bulletin board.
Two coworkers went on “sick leave” at the same time for three days and came back with matching tans. Their work was on you the whole time.
The intern confesses he’s in love with someone in Accounting and asks how to invite her for coffee. It’s 7 p.m.
In the shared calendar, you spot the boss’s meeting with an employee: “Dinner. Just us.” The whole team can see it.
On a new project, you’ll be working with a former classmate you once dated. Coworkers already know.
Rumor says the company driver chauffeurs not just management but also his sweetheart from Sales. You’ve seen it yourself.
HR sent out a survey on workplace relationships: “Are you aware of coworkers’ romances?” It isn’t anonymous.
In the evening, a coworker sends you a long message confessing feelings. Tomorrow you’re presenting together to the boss.
A coworker reads cards for the team about “office love.” You get “the king of diamonds from IT.” The sysadmin blushes.
right: Ask her to put them away

text: Morning. It’s 62°F in the office because the AC was set by a coworker who’s always hot. She took the remote with her to a meeting.
right: Find the remote in her desk

text: July, 84°F in the office. The coworker by the window forbids the AC: “I’ll catch a chill.” The other nine people quietly melt.
The morning starts with the window war. One coworker opens it “for air,” another closes it “for the draft.” Your desk is right in between.
You stumble on the AC remote everyone’s been hunting for a week. It was in the printer paper drawer.
The AC blows right on your neck. Facilities says only the desk can be moved, and that takes a three-page request.
Coworkers hung a thermometer to “settle the debate objectively.” Now they argue about where the thermometer should hang.
A former employee’s ficus sits in the corner, wilting. Nobody wants to water it. The office manager looks at you: “You’re the newest.”
There’s a cactus on your desk from the previous occupant. It’s prickly, in the way, and rumored to bring bad luck. Tossing it feels wrong.
You were away two days, and a coworker watered your plants. With tea. With sugar. The plants seem happy; the ants even more so.
The boss left his palm in your care while on a business trip. It’s shedding leaves before your eyes. He’s back Friday.
A coworker brought an orchid and demands nobody breathe near it. It sits on the shared printer.
A coworker brought a space heater from home. Every time she turns it on, the whole wing blows a fuse.
Morning. At the cooler you learn that your desk neighbor will “soon be fired.” Your neighbor is right there, pouring water.
The office is buzzing: there’ll be cuts, and new hires go first. The only new hire on your team is you.
Zoya brings a new rumor every day. Today’s is about you: supposedly you’re related to the CEO. You’re secretly a bit pleased.
Through a thin wall, you overhear the boss discussing upcoming bonuses on the phone. Coworkers ask what you heard.
The shared inbox got an anonymous complaint about “whoever eats other people’s food.” Everyone suspects you, since you’re new.
Someone told another department about your report mistake. Only three people knew. One of them is your best work buddy.
You told a coworker you were tired. An hour later, HR asks if it’s true you’re job hunting. The rumor went through five people.
In the restroom one morning, you hear two coworkers discussing your new haircut. Opinions are split. Time to leave the stall.
Rumor: the office is moving to the other end of town. Half the team is already job hunting. You just rented an apartment nearby.
A new coworker joined the team. By noon, coworkers had invented three nicknames for her. They want you to vote for “the best one.”
The assistant whispers that the boss is going through “a rough patch” and you’d better not go in today. You need his signature.
In the smoking area, people are comparing salaries. Turns out you earn the least, even less than the intern. Everyone looks at you.
There’s a rumor the intern only got in through connections. He’s sitting next to you and hears it all. You know it’s not true.
Rumor: you’re getting a new “very strict” boss. Coworkers are panicking. You met him at your interview — he’s actually nice.
A coworker shows everyone another coworker’s vacation photos from social media, loudly commenting. She walks in mid-roast.
Someone accidentally posts a screenshot of a private chat about you in the group chat. It’s deleted a minute later. You read it.
Your yogurt disappeared from the shared fridge. Third time this week. There’s a suspect, but no hard evidence.
A coworker is convinced the boss is eavesdropping through the new “smart” flowerpot. She asks you to check it.
Coworkers invite you to a cafe after work. The only item on the agenda: the new deputy boss. You get along well with him.
The heating came on in October, and the radiator by your desk is scorching. The knob is broken, and the plumber will come “within a month.”
A coworker cranked his fan to max, and your papers flew all over the room. He didn’t notice — headphones.
right: Weigh them down with a stapler

text: A coworker going on vacation hands you care instructions for twelve plants. With watering, feeding, and “talking to them” schedules.
Sun glares on your monitor, so you lower the blinds. The coworker opposite raises them: “I need vitamin D.” All morning long.
left: Turn your back to the window

text: A coworker reheats fish in the shared microwave every day. The whole floor smells like the ocean. The office manager asks you to “drop a gentle hint.”
A huge palm stands in the aisle, and every time you pass, a frond slaps your face. It’s the CEO’s favorite.
Someone fed the office plants coffee grounds “using an internet recipe.” Now the office has gnats. Everyone suspects you.
The new AC has an app, and you’re its admin. Now everyone DMs you “make it warmer” and “make it colder.”
A coworker insists the dead flowers in the vase are “a style.” You saw her forget to water them a month ago.
Your favorite succulent vanished from your desk. A week later, you spot it on a desk in the next department, in a new pot.
A coworker complains about the draft from your open window and pointedly puts on a scarf. Without fresh air, you fall asleep.
The office manager set up a “wish tree”: everyone hangs a note with a dream. The boss reads all the notes.
The office bought plants “to boost morale.” Yours needs watering every three hours or it dies.
Office rumor: the senior specialist role is going not to you, but to a coworker who started a month after you. She acts like she knows nothing.
HR sends out the annual vacation schedule. The veterans took the best weeks. You’re left with November or March.
Last evening before vacation. The boss asks you to finish “just one tiny thing.” It looks like three hours of work.
Night before vacation, flight at 6 a.m. The suitcase isn’t packed, and a coworker urgently asks in chat where the report file is.
Before vacation, you have to hand your work to a coworker. He’s half-listening and scrolling his phone. Next week he’ll be calling you on the beach.
Morning, beach, vacation. Your phone buzzes: the boss tagged you in the work chat: “Where’s the file?” It’s in the shared folder.
Sunday night, first day back tomorrow. 437 unread work emails. You could start sorting them now.
First morning after vacation. Coworkers want to see photos. You have two hundred, all of the sea.
You brought fridge magnets for everyone. They’re all the same, yet coworkers are already fighting over the one “without a defect.”
You got vacation in peak season. Tickets cost triple. A coworker offers a swap: his November for your July.
Morning. The boss says your vacation “needs to shift by two weeks.” Tickets and hotel are paid and non-refundable.
Accounting says your vacation pay will arrive “after the vacation, for technical reasons.” You leave in three days with no money for the trip.
You decided to spend your vacation at home. A coworker calls in the evening: “Since you’re in town, pop into the office for an hour.”
You need to set an auto-reply before vacation. The company template reads like a farewell note: “I am no longer reachable and not responsible for the consequences.”
The boss wants you to take the work laptop on vacation “just in case.” It weighs seven pounds, and you’re traveling with a backpack.
Your flight is delayed six hours. You’re stuck at the airport with your work laptop. You could work or watch a series.
Morning by the sea. A coworker sends a screenshot of a spreadsheet: “Where’s the error?” There’s no error; he just doesn’t get the formula.
right: Ask him to wait a week

text: The team is deciding who’s on duty over the New Year holidays. Everyone else has a family, and you don’t. So it’s “logical” for you.
Friday evening. Coworkers invite you to their country house all weekend to “help in the garden and grill some kebabs.” You dreamed of two days on the couch.
Morning before a long weekend. The boss announces that “by tradition” the team works Saturday to make up hours. The tradition is three years old.
Your vacation request came back for the third time marked “Bad dates.” Nobody says which dates are good.
Last workday before vacation. Coworkers planned a farewell cake, but at 6 p.m. the boss calls a meeting.
You and a coworker are off at the same time, with nobody to cover. The boss asks you to sort it “as friends.” The coworker’s trip: Turkey, with kids.
You’re back from an off-grid hike. Turns out in one week the project changed three leads and two deadlines.
right: Take a day to catch up

text: A week until vacation. Tasks pour in: everyone wants it done “before you leave.”
Instead of vacation, the boss suggests a business trip to the seaside: “You’ll get some rest anyway.” Ten-hour workdays, though.
HR suggests splitting your vacation into six two-day chunks. It’s “more convenient for the team.” You can’t rest in two days.
Evening, vacation, you’re at a concert. The boss calls. Twice. Three times. The music is blasting; all you can hear is your name.
On vacation, you run into a coworker from another department. He suggests “briefly discussing the project” over breakfast. Every day.
You’re back from vacation. A new intern is at your desk, holding your mug. Nobody told you.
right: Take it up with the boss

text: Unused vacation days expire in December. The boss says “now’s not the time.” Now is always.
Monday morning after vacation. Your brain is still on the beach. The boss wants a summary by 10:00, and you can’t remember your password.
A coworker went on vacation and left you her project without a single note. The client calls demanding a report you’ve never heard of.
Friday night, vacation tomorrow. A coworker asks you to cover his Monday shift: “You’re not leaving till noon anyway.”
Morning in the mountains. You have your laptop, but there’s signal only at the summit. The boss expects an email by noon.
You posted vacation photos. The boss liked them and commented: “Resting? What about the report?”
Last night of vacation. Your work calendar already has an 8:30 meeting tomorrow. You could reschedule it.
First morning after the New Year holidays. The office is empty: everyone took a day off. The boss calls asking where the team is.
The boss is leaving on vacation and makes you “acting head” for two weeks. No raise, but you get the keys to his office.
You’re booking your vacation in the evening. A coworker messages that “the best hotels are in another country” and sends a tour three times pricier.
You took one day off. In the morning, a coworker texts: “Are you coming in? We can’t manage without you.”
left: Come in for half a day

text: At lunch, coworkers share vacation plans: Maldives, Bali, the Alps. They ask about yours. You’re visiting your grandma in the village.
You return from vacation late at night. There’s a review meeting in the morning, and you haven’t looked at a single document.
August. Everyone’s on vacation; only you and the boss are in. He’s glad of the company and drops by every half hour to chat about life.
You’ve worked a year without vacation. HR reminds you that “by law you must take time off.” The boss asks you to hold off.
Evening by the sea. Email: “Report needed by nine tomorrow.” You did it, but handed it to a coworker before leaving. He’s silent.
Morning, you’ve got a runny nose and a slight fever. Today’s an important meeting you’ve been invited to for the first time. Stay home?
Your desk neighbor came in with a horrible cold: “I’m not contagious, it’s just allergies.” He sneezes every two minutes.
Evening, you’re on sick leave. The boss writes: “How are you feeling? By the way, could you check one spreadsheet?”
Morning after sick leave. HR wants a doctor’s note, but the clinic misspelled your last name. HR won’t budge.
You’re on sick leave, but a coworker can’t open an important file without you. Only you know the password.
The office first-aid kit has only bandages and pills that expired three years ago. Your head hurts, and stand-up is in ten minutes.
You’re sick but working from home. A coworker messages every half hour: “Where are you? Why aren’t you answering?” You were asleep.
A coworker heard you have a cold and brought over honey and a pot of broth. She didn’t come in, but she’ll be hurt if you don’t invite her.
Half the team is on sick leave. You’re healthy, so three of their projects landed on you. The boss promises to “thank you later.”
Company medical checkup during work hours: a line of a hundred people for one doctor. Work’s on hold, and the boss is nervous.
A coworker’s cold remedy: “garlic in your socks.” The whole team is watching to see if you’ll do it.
Free flu shots in the office. Sign-ups are now, but the line won’t get shorter for an hour.
Evening, you’re under a blanket with a fever. The boss calls personally: “Can you come in tomorrow? Even half a day?”
left: Come in for half a day

text: A coworker went on sick leave and asked you to submit her report. It’s in such shape that it needs a full rewrite.
HR launched a “Healthy Habits” challenge: whoever skips the most fast-food lunches wins a certificate. Today the cafeteria has pizza.
You cough in a meeting, and everyone subtly scoots away. The boss suggests you “sit in the next meeting room on camera.”
Poplar fluff season. Your eyes are watering, and coworkers think you’re crying over a reprimand. The boss asks if you’re okay.
right: Play along, take a day off

text: Evening. Sick leave requires a note from a private clinic, which costs half your paycheck. The boss is willing to “just trust you.”
The office manager takes everyone’s temperature in the morning. Yours is 99°F because you ran from the subway. You’re sent home.
A coworker felt sick at work. The boss asks you to take her home in a taxi. Your report is due in an hour.
You’re on sick leave. The group chat is buzzing: the team is tackling your task, clearly in the wrong direction.
Morning. You’ve lost your voice, and today’s your first call with a major client. A coworker offers to call instead, but he’ll take all the credit.
A coworker hands out vitamins to the whole team from a giant jar. Refusing is awkward, but the pills are the size of walnuts.
Evening. Your little brother, whom you’re babysitting, has a fever. You promised the boss you’d be in at eight.
On the way to work, the sole comes off your shoe. Two blocks to the office, stand-up in twenty minutes.
The boss introduced workplace exercises at 11:00. Everyone stands and waves their arms to upbeat music. You’re mid-way through an important email.
A coworker has been on sick leave for three weeks. The team plans to visit him tonight with oranges. You’re buying the oranges.
Splitting headache since morning. A coworker offers a “magic pill” you’ve never heard of.
Eight hours in an awful chair, and your back hurts. A new chair is promised “next quarter.” There’s a spare one in the boss’s office.
The only doctor’s slot is tomorrow at 10 a.m. The boss asks you to reschedule: “You’re not dying.”
A coworker lectures you all morning on the evils of coffee and offers dandelion-root tea instead. She’s already poured you a mug.
The e-sick-leave system “lost” your note. HR says your sick days will be marked as unexcused absence.
right: Ask HR to sort it out

text: You’re on sick leave, but in the evening a task arrives marked “very urgent.” From the boss. Signed “No offense.”
You’re almost better but still coughing a little. People in the elevator turn away in fear. You could walk up to the ninth floor.
You were at the doctor and missed stand-up. Meanwhile, you got a new task, and a coworker promised on your behalf it’d be done by Wednesday.
Evening, 99.5°F. Tomorrow is the company fun run you signed up for a month ago. Coworkers are counting on you for the relay.
The team is in quarantine, everyone working from home. An hour later, the boss asks you specifically to come in for some documents.
A coworker came back from sick leave to find you’d submitted his report. The boss praised you. The coworker is gloomy.
Evening, you’ve got a cold, and coworkers invite you to a birthday at the bowling alley. You promised a week ago.
The new hire you’re training got sick on day one. The boss thinks it’s your fault.
HR calls your home to verify you’re really sick. Your mom answers and tells them all about your “weak immune system” since childhood.
A week on sick leave. You’re bored, so one evening you write in the work chat: “Anything I can do?” Coworkers are already replying.
Payday morning. Everyone in the team chat writes “It’s in!” — but yours isn’t. Accounting opens in an hour.
Your paycheck is $20 short. Accounting explains it’s a “deduction for a broken mug.” You didn’t break it.
Payday evening. Coworkers want to celebrate at a bar. You can afford either the bar or your internet bill.
Three days to payday, $5 in your wallet. A coworker invites you to lunch at a new cafe where the lunch special is $12.
A coworker wants to borrow $100 till payday. Last time he paid you back after six months, $2 at a time.
Evening. Rent and internet bills on the table. Your salary barely covers them. A coworker texts: “Concert on Saturday?”
Morning email: “Salary indexation this year: 0%.” Below it: “But we have new coffee pods!”
You’ve decided to ask the boss for a raise. He’s in a good mood, but leaves for a meeting in ten minutes.
A bonus arrived in the evening. Small but nice. Coworkers who didn’t get one are moping in the group chat.
A coworker spends the day explaining his cashback system: five cards, twelve categories, a three-page spreadsheet. He offers to teach you.
You’ve decided to save money and bring lunch from home. At lunchtime, the whole team heads to a cafe and invites you along.
Evening budget check: you spent more on takeout coffee this month than on utilities. The office machine only makes sludge.
Morning. Salaries are delayed a week “for technical reasons.” The boss asks everyone to “be understanding and not make noise.”
The company offers employees a gym discount. The gym is across town, and the discount is just five percent.
Evening, the team is staying late. Pizza is ordered “split evenly.” You eat the least but pay the same.
You read your pay stub carefully for the first time. There are mystery lines: “Hazard bonus” and “Joy deduction.”
A coworker swears you can “double your salary in a month” with some investment course. The course costs half your salary.
Evening, an online store is having a sale. You’re eyeing a home coffee machine that would pay for itself in six months. Payday was today.
In the morning, your transit card is empty and can only be topped up with cash. No cash. A coworker lives nearby and drives.
A coworker discovered tax refunds and now helps everyone file. He caught you at lunch: “It’s only half an hour!”
Payday evening. You want to buy expensive headphones. Your conscience says save for vacation.
Morning, the team’s “Win a Day’s Pay” raffle. A ticket costs $2. Someone from Accounting always wins.
A coworker you lent money to is showing off his new phone. He seems to have forgotten the debt.
Evening at a cafe with coworkers. The bill is split “evenly,” but you only had soup. They ordered steaks.
Morning. You plan to save money and bring lunch. Coworkers joke that “a lunchbox is an admission of poverty.” Lunch is already packed.
The company is switching banks. You have to get a card at a branch during work hours. The line takes half a day.
Evening at a cafe with coworkers. Everyone leaves a different tip. You feel like they expect the most from you.
The boss announced raises for everyone except you: “You’re still on probation.” Probation ended a month ago.
The boss borrowed $20 from you “till tonight.” That night was a week ago, but asking is awkward.
The electric bill arrived, double the usual. You remember heating the apartment with a space heater all winter.
Morning financial-literacy seminar. The speaker recommends saving half your salary. Coworkers laugh out loud.
In the shared folder, you stumble on a file with the whole team’s salaries. A coworker your age earns one and a half times more.
Evening. Your banking app says you’ve saved exactly half for vacation. Coworkers invite you to the movies.
A coworker asks you to break a $100 bill. You only have coins. He shuffles off, offended, to the next desk.
In the cafeteria, a coworker loudly complains about low pay. The boss is at the next table. The coworker asks you to back him up.
In your pocket you find a receipt: you paid for the whole team at a cafe a week ago. Nobody paid you back.
right: Write it off as a gift

text: A stack of cafeteria discount coupons arrived at the office. You got there first, and the stack is yours. Coworkers want some too.
The boss promises a bonus for the best cost-saving idea. You know one: cancel pointless meetings. His meetings.
Friday evening. A friend offers you weekend work as a courier. Good money, but no weekend.
In the morning, you get a transfer from a stranger labeled “Thanks for the help.” A minute later a coworker calls: “Wrong number, please send it back.”
The company will pay for one subscription per employee: a streaming service or an Excel course. The boss is watching who picks what.
You decided to track your budget in a spreadsheet. An hour later, it’s done, and it turns out “little things” eat a third of your salary.
A coworker suggests a “coffee fund”: everyone chips in for good coffee. The treasurer, naturally, will be you.
The cafeteria raised prices. Coworkers are boycotting it for a week by eating at the cafe across the street. The cafe is pricier.
Evening, you decided to treat yourself “a little” online. Half an hour later, your cart equals your salary. The cursor hovers over “Pay.”
On the subway, you’re finishing a freelance job: a bakery logo. The client wants “a croissant, but serious.” Due by lunch.
Evening. The freelance client asks for revisions a fifth time: “Like the first version, only different.” You have an early start.
right: Put it off to the weekend

text: You sell knitted hats online. A coworker found your shop and wants a hat with a “friends discount.”
Your side job at a night cafe pays well. Tonight’s shift runs till 2 a.m., and there’s an important stand-up in the morning.
You deliver orders by bike before work. Today’s route goes right past the boss’s windows.
Your houseplant blog hit a thousand followers. Coworkers found out and now want you to save their ficuses at lunch.
You tutor a ninth-grader in English in the evenings. His mom wants two more sessions a week “at the old rate.”
You learn that a coworker drives a taxi on weekends. He drove you on Saturday, and you didn’t notice.
A freelance client calls during work hours demanding a file right now. The boss is walking past your desk.
You make candles to sell in the evenings. The apartment smells of vanilla, and tomorrow’s report isn’t even started.
HR asks if you have a side job: “It’s just for the form, no big deal.” She clearly knows something.
A coworker suggests reselling sneakers together: “We each put in $100, in a month we get $400.” He’s already buried in boxes.
Friday evening. You and a friend run a stall at the weekend market. Coworkers found out and promised to come “show support,” i.e., gawk.
You got up at 5 a.m. to finish an order. It’s done, but you’re nodding off over your notebook at stand-up.
A side-gig client left you a nasty, unfair review. Coworkers saw it and offer to “bury it in good reviews.”
Evening. You tally it up: sixty hours this week across two jobs. Friends invite you to a birthday party.
Your home printer broke, and you need to print twenty pages for an order. The office printer is free.
A coworker learned you build websites and wants one for his mother-in-law. For free, “as a friend.”
You teach an online drawing class to fifteen students in the evening. The boss calls an unscheduled meeting.
Morning. A client wants you to give a presentation to his company at 11:00. You have a meeting with the boss then.
left: Ask the boss for time off

text: A coworker, inspired by your shop, opened an identical one — same hats, lower price. He’s proudly showing it to everyone.
Evening. You’re writing cheap copy for clients. The boss sends a work question right as your copy deadline hits.
In the morning, the boss shows you your own freelance profile. “When do you find the time?” he asks with a smile.
You spend lunch breaks shipping side-gig parcels. Coworkers think you’re avoiding them.
You bake custom cakes on weekends. On Friday evening, a coworker orders one for tomorrow — “for three hundred people.”
You teach a guitar lesson by video before work. The student is twenty minutes late, and now you might be late too.
You’re asked to work your side job on Saturday, the day of the office team building. The gig pays double.
Evening. An overseas client wants a call at midnight your time. He offers extra pay for the inconvenience.
In the morning, the boss is wearing a hat you knitted and sold online. He’s praising it to the whole team.
A coworker wants to start freelancing and asks you to show him the ropes. “Half an hour at lunch, tops.” It’s been two hours.
In the evening, you’re offered a steady half-day side job with good pay. You’d have to leave your main job at 3 p.m.
The courier delivering office lunches turns out to be your coworker from Accounting. He begs you not to tell anyone.
You built a website for your side gig. A coworker noticed you used photos of the office in the “About Us” section.
Evening. Forty orders for your keychains came in on the marketplace. Each has to be packed by morning.
Morning. A side-gig client calls during stand-up. Five times. Everyone stares at your phone.
HR sent a memo banning side jobs “that harm your main job.” You’re reading it with a gig open on your second monitor.
Evening. Your math student aced his test. His parents want to give you a cake. Your diet starts tomorrow.
In the morning, you remember you didn’t pay tax on your side income. It’s due today, and the tax site barely loads.
right: Go to the tax office at lunch

text: Your coworker also freelances and stole a client from you by halving the price. Today he’s sitting opposite, smiling sweetly.
You’re hosting a webinar for your blog followers. Two hundred people joined, including your boss under the handle “Observer.”
You arrive at the office with a huge courier backpack. Coworkers joke you’re “off on a hike.” Security eyes it suspiciously.
Not knowing who you are on the freelance site, the boss ordered business-card designs from you. The meeting with “the designer” is tomorrow.
Evening. Friends are opening a coffee shop and want you as a weekend barista. Pay: coffee and gratitude.
After a night gig, you arrive at the office with dark circles. The boss asks “how you slept.”
A coworker sells cosmetics right in the office all day. Today she offers to make you her “distributor.”
Friday evening. Your main job is celebrating the end of the quarter, and your side gig has an urgent order on fire.
In the morning, both your main job and your gig have tasks on fire. Both are “urgent and important.”
You bring your paintings to the office to sell to coworkers. The boss picks one and asks for a “management discount.”
Friday evening. A client will pay triple for weekend work. Your friends already bought tickets for a trip out of town.
The company paid for your online course “Effective Communication.” Every morning at 7:30: a forty-minute lesson and a quiz.
A mandatory evening webinar on the new accounting system. The speaker has been reading slides aloud for three hours. Cameras on.
right: Put up a photo of yourself

text: The boss wants everyone safety-certified by month’s end. A hundred-question test, passing score ninety.
Morning sales training. The coach calls you up to “sell me this pen” in front of the team. The pen doesn’t write.
The company-paid English classes run three evenings a week till nine. It’s Friday, and friends invite you to the movies.
You’re asked to train three interns, though you’ve only been here a month yourself. You have lunch hour to prepare.
You finished an Excel course and now know pivot tables. Coworkers found out and lined up with their files first thing.
Tomorrow morning is the certification exam your raise depends on. Coworkers invite you to a birthday dinner at a restaurant.
The office brought in a time-management expert. The lecture runs three hours and wrecked everyone’s deadlines for the day.
The boss hands out “How to Become Indispensable” and will ask Friday what you took from it. It’s four hundred pages.
You’re offered six months of evening training courses. A promotion is promised afterward. Possibly.
The team takes a product-knowledge test. You score 54 out of 100. The boss posts the rankings on the wall.
In the morning, you find the corporate ethics course was due yesterday. The system sent a reminder to your boss.
You decided to learn programming tonight. Two hours later, “Hello, world!” is on the screen, and you’re incredibly proud.
You’ve been assigned a mentor. He teaches you “the right way to work,” but following his advice means redoing every report.
At your public-speaking class, you’re asked to speak on “the most boring object.” You chose a stapler.
Evening. You passed your course, and the instructor asks you to post about it on social media with the company tag.
The team is watching a fire-safety training film from 1987. The boss is noting who falls asleep.
In the morning, a coworker hangs her fifth certificate above her desk. You have none. The boss nods approvingly.
Evening, mandatory course. The videos can’t be skipped, and every block ends with a quiz. There are twelve blocks.
right: Play it and go eat dinner

text: A company-paid “mindfulness” workshop at lunch. The boss is already there, waving at you.
The company offers a free analytics course on Saturdays from 9 a.m. The certificate is “highly valued for promotions.”
Evening. You’re reading an accounting textbook to understand your work better. A coworker texts: “Are you transferring to Accounting?”
In a week there’s the review that decides whether you stay after probation. Questions are secret, but a coworker offers last year’s.
A webinar starts at 8 a.m., and you join from home in pajamas. Suddenly the host asks everyone to turn on cameras.
Evening leadership course. The coach splits everyone into groups and makes you leader. Your boss is in your group.
After a time-management course, you built the perfect schedule. An hour later, the boss dropped three urgent tasks outside it.
Your online yoga class overlaps with stand-up. The instructor is horrified by your pose; the boss, by your background.
Evening. You’re writing a term paper for your part-time degree. The topic is suspiciously close to your work project. You could use work materials.
You’re being sent to a conference in another city to give a twenty-minute talk, though you’ve only been here three months.
right: Ask them to send someone else

text: The boss announces a test on the new procedures at 9:00. The procedures were emailed at 8:45. Thirty pages.
Evening art classes are your outlet. Today the boss asks you to stay for a “quick” meeting at 6:30.
The company launches “Friday Lectures”: once a month, everyone teaches coworkers something useful. Your turn is tomorrow.
Your course certificate arrives by email. Your last name is misspelled and the date is wrong. The boss wants it printed.
You’re asked to record a training video for the interns. Camera: your phone. Lighting: a desk lamp. Take: nine.
After the negotiation course, coworkers notice you say “Let’s explore your interests” even about the microwave line.
HR reminds you of study leave for exams. The boss asks you to “somehow juggle both.”
Evening exam session at your part-time university. The professor is an hour late, and you’re due at work at eight.
You found a great design course, but the company won’t pay for it. It costs a month’s salary.
Your mentor wants you to practice on a real client. It’s the most difficult client in the company.
Evening, course homework. A coworker offers his answers; he took the course last year.
The boss wants the whole team certified. Those who passed must “coach” those who didn’t. You passed.
You’re watching a mandatory video course on “company culture.” It shows the office you’re sitting in, ten years ago.
Evening, you got an online “Project Manager” diploma. Coworkers in the chat ask if “it’s even real.”
New Year party night. The CEO hands out “Employee of the Year” certificates. Your last name is mispronounced, and the room laughs.
The party’s over, and the venue must be cleared by eleven. The organizer asks the young folks to help with garlands and chairs.
HR announces you can bring a “plus-one” to the party. The chat instantly starts guessing who everyone will bring.
Night before the “Pirates” theme party. No costume, stores are closing. In the closet: striped pajamas and Grandma’s shawl.
Monday after the retreat. The coworker who caught you in the “trust fall” jokes all morning about your “unique center of gravity.”
Evening. The collection for the boss’s milestone birthday closes tomorrow. It’s $200 short. Coworkers hint that “whoever has no mortgage can cover it.”
Cafeteria whispers: Sales will merge with your department, and someone will have to go. People ask if you know anything.
Leaving in the evening, you notice the AC set to 61°F. Tomorrow, the coworker who set it will show up in a fur coat and complain again.
Morning after vacation. Your tasks were given to others, and you’re left with “sorting the archive” — five years of it.
Evening. The boss is sick and calls from home: he wants you to run tomorrow’s meeting with partners for him.
Smoking-area talk: new hires get a raise starting this month. Nobody told you anything. Coworkers advise you to “fight for yours.”
In the evening, you accidentally posted a message to your freelance client in the work chat: “Mockup almost done, discount still on.” The boss already read it.
You rush to your English class before work. The teacher runs half an hour over, and stand-up is at 9:00.
Evening email: “Congratulations! You’ve earned a Leadership Certificate.” You never took the course. Seems like a mailing error.
The birthday boy invited the team to lunch at a restaurant. In the end, the bill is split evenly, including him.
Evening after karaoke with coworkers. Your voice is shot, and tomorrow morning is your first client presentation.
Two coworkers are fighting over whose plant gets the best spot on the windowsill. The windowsill is by your desk.
left: Give it to the first one

text: The secret admirer left another chocolate bar. Today with a note: “Meet me at the cooler at 6 p.m.” It’s 5:55.
A coworker going on vacation asks you to “just check the inbox.” Day one: two hundred client emails.
Evening message from HR: “You didn’t sign consent to attend the team building.” It was yesterday. You were there.
A collection for a coworker’s wedding is announced: $60 each. A week to payday, $100 on your card.
Night before your vacation. Nobody will take the ficus you’ve been caring for. Coworkers decline one by one.
The company paid for a stress-management course. The session is scheduled exactly at your deadline.
Evening. A side-gig client will pay double if the website is ready by morning. You have your performance review in the morning.
In the morning, the security guard hands you a huge box: “For you, from an admirer.” Inside, a giant stuffed elephant. Coworkers gather at your desk.
Evening. A close friend asks to borrow a big sum till spring. It’s exactly the vacation money you’ve saved for six months.
The department head is leaving. Coworkers want to give him “something funny.” Your idea is a hit, but it’s all on you to execute.
Friday night, bar with coworkers. At the end, someone suggests “paying with your bonus.” You’re the one who got a bonus, it seems.
Morning after two coworkers’ wedding. The newlyweds are back at work, sharing a desk. The boss asks you to “make sure they work.”
At your evening English class, you spot the coworker who told everyone he’s “perfectly fluent.” He’s in the beginners’ group.
Facilities password-locked the AC. Rumor says only your boss knows the code. It’s 86°F in the office.
Evening, you stayed late. The last bus leaves in ten minutes. A coworker asks you to “quickly celebrate” his promotion.
Morning after an office birthday. There’s a salad in the fridge that nobody can remember the origin of.
Your paycheck arrives in the evening. A minute later, a bank text: “Charge for a course subscription you forgot to cancel.”
You want the company to pay for a design course. The boss says you need a five-page justification first.
A coworker sends you a long DM about who fell out with whom on the team. You haven’t had dinner yet.
In the morning, it turns out someone “borrowed till tonight” the money from the gift envelope. You were keeping it.
December 31, evening. You’ve been asked to stay on duty at the office till ten. The boss promises a day off “sometime later.”
HR asks if you want premium health insurance at half price. Half price is a quarter of your salary.
Friday evening. A coworker brought a guitar and suggests staying to sing. Security locks the building at eight.
Monday morning, you’re on vacation. A coworker calls: “Oh, aren’t you at work?” — and immediately asks for some advice.
In the evening, the intern gives you a card: “Thanks for teaching me!” You barely explained anything, but it’s touching.
An important client has arrived, and the meeting room is 54°F thanks to the AC. The remote has been missing a month.
At the gym with the corporate discount, you run into the boss. He suggests “working out together.” Every evening.
You learn your course certificate must be picked up in person at the training center. It’s only open till 10 a.m.
In the evening, you meet a neighbor who works at your company. She shares gossip about your department you’ve never heard.
You’ve earned a day off for being on duty. Coworkers ask you to take Friday so Saturday’s trip isn’t ruined. You wanted Monday.
Evening. You remember today is the boss’s birthday, and you didn’t wish him well. Forty minutes to midnight.
The boss ceremoniously hands you a course certificate. Coworkers who didn’t pass exchange sour looks.
Friday evening. The team proposes a ritual: everyone says aloud what they’re grateful to coworkers for this week. It’s your turn.
